tool.name: GitLab CI/CD
tool.tagline: GitLab's built-in pipelines: build, test and deploy from .gitlab-ci.yml
tool.description: GitLab CI/CD runs pipelines defined in a .gitlab-ci.yml file at the root of a GitLab repository. Jobs are grouped into stages, executed by runners (usually inside Docker images), and can pass artifacts, deploy to environments and trigger other pipelines. It is the standard way to automate builds, tests and deployments for teams that host their code on GitLab.com or a self-managed GitLab.

glossary.def: In GitLab CI/CD, one named piece of work in a pipeline: a list of shell commands that a runner carries out, usually inside a fresh container.
A group of jobs in a GitLab pipeline. All jobs in a stage run at the same time; the next stage starts only when they have all succeeded.
A program, usually on another machine, that keeps asking GitLab for jobs and carries them out, typically each in a fresh Docker container.
The program you install on your own machines to run GitLab CI/CD jobs. It asks GitLab for work and runs each job with an executor.
The method a GitLab runner uses to run each job: in a fresh Docker container, on a Kubernetes cluster, directly on the machine, or on a new cloud virtual machine.
A label given to a GitLab runner, such as gpu or linux. A job that lists tags is only taken by a runner that has all of them.
A named value GitLab hands to a job's scripts as an environment variable, set in .gitlab-ci.yml or in the project's settings.
A variable GitLab sets automatically in every job, such as CI_COMMIT_SHA (the commit) or CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE (why the pipeline started).
An extra container GitLab starts next to a job, such as a database the tests need. The job reaches it by a name taken from its image.
Running a Docker daemon inside a container (the docker:dind image), so a job that itself runs in a container can build images.
A container given full access to the machine it runs on, almost like its administrator. Needed for Docker-in-Docker, and risky.
A GitLab job that waits in the pipeline until someone clicks to start it, often used for production deploys.
A set of steps joined by one-way arrows that never loop back, showing what must finish before what. Pipelines using needs: form one.
A GitLab CI/CD variable whose value is replaced with [MASKED] wherever it would appear in job logs.
A branch (or tag) that only trusted people may push to, usually main and release branches. Protected variables and runners serve only these.
A GitLab CI/CD variable given only to pipelines running on protected branches or tags, so other branches can't read it.
A temporary password GitLab creates for each job (CI_JOB_TOKEN), letting it use registries and parts of the GitLab API until the job ends.
A reusable, versioned piece of GitLab pipeline configuration with declared inputs, published in the CI/CD Catalog and pulled in with include.
GitLab's searchable list of published CI/CD components that projects can reuse.
A GitLab job whose name starts with a dot, such as .test-base. It never runs; other jobs copy its settings with extends.
A GitLab CI keyword that makes a job inherit settings from one or more other, usually hidden, jobs. Lists such as script are replaced, not joined.
A temporary running copy of an app created for one branch or merge request, so reviewers can try the change before it's merged.
A GitLab setting (resource_group) that lets only one job of the group run at a time across all pipelines, so two deploys never overlap.
A GitLab environment, such as production, whose deploy jobs only chosen people may run, optionally after an approval.
A GitLab job that starts another pipeline (a child pipeline or one in another project) instead of running a script.
A pipeline started by a trigger job of another pipeline: a child pipeline in the same project, or a pipeline in another project.
A pipeline started from a trigger job in the same project, with its own stages and jobs, shown nested inside its parent pipeline.
A pipeline in one GitLab project that a trigger job in another project's pipeline starts.
One fact stated inside a signed token such as a JWT, for example which project or branch the token was issued for.
The rule on the cloud's side saying which signed tokens it accepts, for example only those from one project's main branch.
A GitLab pipeline run for a commit pushed to a branch (CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE is push).
A GitLab pipeline run for a merge request's source branch when the merge request is opened or updated.
A GitLab pipeline that tests a temporary commit combining a merge request with the latest target branch, as the code would be after merging.
A GitLab queue of merge requests where each one is tested on top of the target branch plus all merge requests ahead of it, then merged in order.
GitLab's page for editing .gitlab-ci.yml in the browser; it checks the file as you type and shows the fully merged configuration.

concepts.name: Pipelines, stages, jobs and runners
concepts.summary: The building blocks of GitLab CI/CD: a pipeline of stages, each holding jobs, which runners carry out.
concepts.why: Every .gitlab-ci.yml file is written in these terms, and they decide what runs at the same time and where.
concepts.body:
Every time someone pushes a commit, a team wants the same checks: does the code still build, do the tests still pass? And if all is well, the new version should go live. Doing that by hand is slow and gets forgotten. **CI/CD** automates it: continuous integration (CI) checks every change automatically, and continuous delivery or deployment (CD) ships it. GitLab, a Git hosting service like GitHub, has this built in.

You describe the work in a file named `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the top of your repository. Each time you push (or on a schedule, or when you click **Run pipeline**), GitLab reads the file and starts a **pipeline**: one complete run of all the steps for that commit.

A pipeline is made of **jobs**: named pieces of work, each with a `script`, a list of shell commands to run. Jobs are grouped into **stages** that run in order: by default `build`, then `test`, then `deploy`. All jobs in one stage run at the same time; the next stage starts only when every job of the previous stage has succeeded. A job without a `stage` goes into `test`.

Jobs are carried out by **runners**: programs on other machines that keep asking GitLab for work. GitLab.com provides hosted runners, and companies often add their own. Most runners start each job in a fresh Docker container, from an image you choose.

On GitLab's website, under **Build, Pipelines**, you can watch a pipeline, read each job's output and download files it produced. The result, passed or failed, is also shown next to the commit and on **merge requests**: GitLab's name for a request to merge one branch into another after review (GitHub calls them pull requests). A team can require a passing pipeline before anything is merged.

Because each job starts in a clean container, jobs share nothing by default. A file made in one job is gone in the next, unless you pass it on as an artifact (a later lesson).
concepts.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml: three stages, four jobs
stages: [build, test, deploy]

build-app:
  stage: build
  script: echo "compiling"

unit-tests:            # these two run at the same time
  stage: test
  script: echo "unit tests"
lint:
  stage: test
  script: echo "checking code style"

deploy-prod:           # starts after both test jobs pass
  stage: deploy
  script: echo "deploying"
takeaways: A pipeline has stages; a stage has jobs; runners carry out the jobs
Jobs in a stage run at the same time; stages run one after another
Each job starts in a clean container
pitfalls: Assuming a file created in the build job is automatically present in the test job.

quiz.q: A job in the test stage fails. What happens to the jobs in the deploy stage?
options: They run only if allow_failure is set on deploy
They run at the same time as test
quiz.explain: A stage starts only after all jobs of the previous stage succeeded (unless a failure was marked as allowed).

concepts.name: Your first .gitlab-ci.yml
concepts.summary: Write a pipeline that installs what your code needs and runs its tests in a Docker image, then watch it run after a push.
concepts.why: A green (passing) pipeline on every push is the first step to merging changes with confidence.
concepts.body:
Create a file named `.gitlab-ci.yml` in the top folder of your repository, commit it and push. GitLab reads it and starts a pipeline straight away. If the file has a mistake, the pipeline page says so, and the **Pipeline editor** (Build, Pipeline editor) checks the file while you type.

The file is written in **YAML**, a plain text format of `name: value` lines. Indentation (spaces at the start of a line) shows what belongs inside what, and lines starting with `- ` are items in a list.

Each top-level name that isn't one of GitLab's own settings (like `stages` or `default`) defines a job. The essentials inside a job:

- `script`: one command, or a list of commands, run by the runner's shell. If any command ends with a non-zero exit code, the job fails.
- `image`: the Docker image the job runs in, such as `python:3.13` or `node:22`.
- `before_script` and `after_script`: commands run before and after `script`. `after_script` runs even when the job failed, in a separate shell.

A `default:` section sets `image`, `before_script` and similar settings once, for every job.

Each job starts with your repository already cloned into a folder whose path is in the `$CI_PROJECT_DIR` environment variable, so there's no download step to write. To save time, GitLab fetches only the latest 20 commits of history.

Watch out for one YAML trap: a command containing `: ` (a colon followed by a space), or starting with a special character such as `*` or `{`, must be put in quotes, or YAML reads it as a `name: value` pair instead of a command. When in doubt, quote the whole command.
concepts.code:
default:
  image: python:3.13-slim

stages: [test]

test:
  stage: test
  before_script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt   # install the packages the project needs
  script:
    - python -m pytest -q        # run the tests: 12 passed in 0.8s
    - "echo 'Result: done'"      # quoted because of the colon-space
  after_script:
    - echo "always runs, even on failure"
takeaways: Commit .gitlab-ci.yml at the top of the repository and push to start a pipeline
script is required; image picks the container
The code is already cloned into $CI_PROJECT_DIR
pitfalls: Unquoted commands containing ': ' break the YAML file.

quiz.q: Your job's second script command fails. What happens to after_script?
options: It runs only if allow_failure is true
quiz.explain: after_script always runs after script, success or failure, in a separate shell.

concepts.name: Images, services and default settings
concepts.summary: Pick a Docker image per job, start helper containers such as databases with services, and share settings with default.
concepts.why: Tests usually need specific tools and a real database; services provide the database without setting up any servers.
concepts.body:
Every job runs inside the image named by `image`. Pin a version tag (`postgres:17`, `node:22-alpine`) rather than `latest`, so the pipeline behaves the same next month. Images can come from Docker Hub, from GitLab's own container registry for your project (its address is in `$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE`), or from any registry the runner can reach.

Tests often need other programs running next to them, most often a **database**: a program that stores data, such as PostgreSQL. **Service containers**, or services, are extra containers GitLab starts alongside the job for this. The job reaches a service by its network name, its **hostname**, taken from the image name (`postgres:17` becomes `postgres`), or by a name you choose with `alias`. Service containers also receive the job's `variables`, which is how you set the database's password.

`default:` applies settings to every job unless a job sets its own: `image`, `services`, `before_script`, `after_script`, `tags`, `retry` (re-run a failed job automatically), `timeout` and a few others.

Building a Docker image inside a job is a special case: the job already runs in a container, yet needs a Docker daemon to talk to. Two common patterns:

- start a `docker:dind` service. **Docker-in-Docker** is a Docker daemon running inside a container. It needs a runner that allows **privileged containers**, which get full access to the machine they run on.
- use a builder that needs no daemon at all, such as BuildKit's standalone mode or Kaniko.

To push the image to your project's registry, GitLab gives every job `$CI_REGISTRY`, `$CI_REGISTRY_USER` and `$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD`, so you never have to store a password yourself.
concepts.code:
default:
  image: python:3.13-slim
  retry: 1

integration:
  services:
    - name: postgres:17
      alias: db
  variables:
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test       # also passed to the service container
    DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:test@db:5432/postgres
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest tests/integration

build-image:
  image: docker:28
  services: [docker:28-dind]
  script:
    - docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" -p "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" "$CI_REGISTRY"
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA" .
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"
takeaways: image sets the job's container; pin its tag
services start helper containers, reached by name or alias
default: shares image, before_script, retry and more across jobs
pitfalls: Connecting to localhost (the job's own container) to reach a service: each service has its own hostname.

quiz.q: A job has services: [redis:7]. Which hostname reaches Redis by default?
quiz.explain: By default the service's name comes from the image name without the tag.

concepts.name: CI/CD variables and predefined variables
concepts.summary: Define variables in YAML, use GitLab's predefined CI_ variables, and know which value wins when a name is set twice.
concepts.why: Variables carry the branch, the commit and your settings into scripts; almost every rule and script uses them.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name that stands for a value. **CI/CD variables** are environment variables that GitLab hands to your job's scripts. Define them with `variables:` at the top level (for all jobs) or inside one job (for that job only, replacing a top-level value with the same name).

GitLab also sets many **predefined variables** in every job:

- `CI_COMMIT_SHA`, `CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA`: the commit ID, in full and shortened.
- `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH`: the branch name. It's empty in pipelines for a Git tag (a permanent name such as `v1.2.0` that marks a release), and in **merge request pipelines**, which run for a merge request rather than for a plain push. `CI_COMMIT_TAG` holds the tag name in tag pipelines; `CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME` holds the branch or tag name, whichever applies.
- `CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH`: the repository's main branch, usually `main`.
- `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE`: why the pipeline exists: `push`, `merge_request_event`, `schedule`, `web` (someone clicked Run pipeline), `trigger`, `api`...
- `CI_PROJECT_DIR`, `CI_JOB_ID`, `CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE`, and `CI_JOB_TOKEN` (a temporary password for this job, covered later).

Variables can also be set outside the file: in the settings of a project, of a group (GitLab's folders of projects) or of the whole GitLab server; for a scheduled pipeline; or when you start a pipeline by hand. When the same name is set in several places, values from settings or typed in by hand win over the file, and a job's own value wins over the top-level one.

A variable can use other variables (`IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA`). GitLab fills these in before the job starts for some settings (like `image` or `rules`), and the shell fills them in inside `script`. To see everything a job receives, run `export` in a test job, but never in a project with secrets, because they would be printed in the log.
concepts.code:
variables:                       # all jobs
  APP_NAME: shop
  IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

show:
  variables:
    APP_NAME: shop-api            # overrides the global value for this job
  script:
    - echo "$APP_NAME $IMAGE"     # shop-api registry.gitlab.com/acme/shop:1a2b3c4d
    - echo "source=$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE branch=$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH"
    # source=push branch=main
takeaways: variables: at the top level or per job; the job's value wins
CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE and CI_COMMIT_BRANCH drive most logic
Values from settings or typed in by hand beat values in the file
pitfalls: Using CI_COMMIT_BRANCH in a merge request pipeline: it's empty there; use CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME or CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME.

quiz.q: Which variable tells you a pipeline was started by a merge request?
quiz.explain: CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE records the trigger; merge request pipelines have the value merge_request_event.

concepts.name: Controlling when jobs run with rules
concepts.summary: Use rules with if, changes and exists to add jobs only when needed, make them manual, and control whole pipelines with workflow:rules.
concepts.why: Without rules every job runs on every push; with them you deploy only from main and skip work nobody needs.
concepts.body:
`rules` decides whether a job is added to a pipeline at all. GitLab checks the list **in order**, and the first rule that matches wins; if none match, the job is **not added**. Each rule can test:

- `if`: a condition on variables, such as `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH`, or `$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+/`. Here `=~` checks a **regular expression**, a text pattern: this one means "starts with v and a digit".
- `changes`: files changed by the push, written as paths or **glob patterns**, where `*` stands for any name (`src/**/*` means everything under `src`).
- `exists`: files present in the repository.

A matching rule can set `when`: `on_success` (the default: run if earlier stages passed), `manual` (a **manual job**: it waits until someone clicks), `delayed` (wait for the time set by `start_in`), `always` or `never`. It can also set `allow_failure` (a failure doesn't stop the pipeline) and `variables`.

A common pattern is to rule out cases first with `when: never` rules, then end with a rule that matches everything else. `workflow:rules` uses the same syntax for the **whole pipeline**: if no rule matches, no pipeline is created. Its most common use is avoiding two pipelines for one push when the branch has an open merge request.

`rules` replaces the older `only` and `except` keywords. They still work, but can't be combined with `rules` in the same job; new configuration should use `rules` everywhere.
concepts.code:
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never                       # avoid branch + MR duplicate pipelines
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH || $CI_COMMIT_TAG

docs:
  script: make docs
  rules:
    - changes: ["docs/**/*"]            # only when docs changed

deploy:
  script: ./deploy.sh
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual                      # needs a click on main
    - when: never                       # nowhere else
takeaways: The first matching rule wins; no match means the job is not added
when: manual, delayed, never and always tune the outcome
workflow:rules decides whether a pipeline is created at all
pitfalls: Mixing rules with only/except in the same job, which is a configuration error.

quiz.q: A job has rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG. You push to a branch. What happens to the job?
options: It is not added to the pipeline
It runs because rules default to always
quiz.explain: No rule matched, so the job is excluded from the pipeline.

concepts.name: Artifacts and cache
concepts.summary: Pass build output to later jobs with artifacts, publish test reports, and speed up installs with a cache keyed on lock files.
concepts.why: Jobs share nothing by default, so artifacts and caches are how pipelines move files and save minutes.
concepts.body:
**Artifacts** are files a job produces that GitLab keeps: `artifacts: paths:` lists them, and `expire_in` sets how long they're kept. By default, jobs in later stages download the artifacts of all jobs in earlier stages; `dependencies:` or `needs:` limit that. You can also browse and download artifacts on GitLab's website.

`artifacts:reports` are artifacts GitLab knows how to read. For example, `junit` test results (JUnit XML, a common test-report file format) are shown right in the merge request, and there are report types for test coverage, code quality and security scanners. Add `when: always` so reports are uploaded even when tests fail.

A **cache** keeps downloaded dependencies from one pipeline to the next, so they don't have to be downloaded again. It's stored on the runner (or in shared cloud storage) and is best-effort: it may be missing at any time. Configure `cache: key:` (the cache's name) and `paths:`. With `key: files: [package-lock.json]`, the name is computed from a **lock file**, the file listing the exact package versions, so the cache starts fresh whenever the dependencies change. `policy: pull` on jobs that only read the cache skips the slow upload at the end.

The rule: **artifacts** pass results to later jobs and to people; the **cache** only speeds things up. Never rely on the cache for correctness.

A **package manager** (a tool such as pip or npm that downloads packages) should keep its download folder inside the project, for example `PIP_CACHE_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip`, because only paths inside `$CI_PROJECT_DIR` can be cached or kept as artifacts.
concepts.code:
variables:
  PIP_CACHE_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip

test:
  image: python:3.13
  cache:
    key:
      files: [requirements.txt]      # new cache when deps change
    paths: [.cache/pip]
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest --junitxml=report.xml
  artifacts:
    when: always                     # upload even if tests fail
    reports:
      junit: report.xml              # shown in the merge request

build:
  stage: build
  script: [make dist]
  artifacts:
    paths: [dist/]
    expire_in: 1 week
takeaways: Artifacts = outputs for later jobs and people; cache = speed-up only
Key caches on lock files with cache:key:files
Only paths inside $CI_PROJECT_DIR can be cached or kept as artifacts
pitfalls: Using the cache to pass build output to a deploy job: the cache may be missing on another runner.

quiz.q: A deploy job must receive the dist/ folder built two stages earlier. What should the build job use?
quiz.explain: Artifacts are reliably passed to later jobs; caches are best-effort.

concepts.name: needs: faster pipelines as a DAG
concepts.summary: Let jobs start as soon as the jobs they depend on finish, ignoring stage order, and choose which artifacts they download.
concepts.why: Stage-by-stage pipelines wait for the slowest job; needs can cut total pipeline time a lot.
concepts.body:
With stages alone, a job waits for **every** job in all earlier stages. `needs:` changes that: a job with `needs: [build-api]` starts as soon as `build-api` succeeds, even if other jobs of earlier stages are still running. The pipeline becomes a **directed acyclic graph** (DAG): steps joined by one-way arrows that never loop back. The pipeline view draws them as lines between jobs.

Details that matter:

- A job with `needs: []` starts immediately when the pipeline is created.
- With `needs`, a job downloads artifacts **only** from the jobs it needs. Use `needs: [{job: build, artifacts: false}]` to wait without downloading.
- If a needed job is not in the pipeline (because its rules excluded it), the pipeline fails to be created, unless the need is marked `optional: true`.
- A job can need up to 50 jobs by default, and can even need jobs in the same stage.

A common use is a **monorepo**, one repository holding several projects, where say the website and the server code each build, test and deploy on their own: each chain moves at its own speed, instead of all website tests waiting for the slowest server build.

Stages still matter as a visual grouping and for jobs without `needs`, so most pipelines combine the two.
concepts.code:
stages: [build, test, deploy]

build-api:  {stage: build, script: [make api],  artifacts: {paths: [api/bin/]}}
build-web:  {stage: build, script: [make web],  artifacts: {paths: [web/dist/]}}

test-api:
  stage: test
  needs: [build-api]          # starts when build-api is done, not build-web
  script: [make test-api]

lint:
  stage: test
  needs: []                   # starts immediately
  script: [make lint]

deploy-web:
  stage: deploy
  needs:
    - job: build-web          # gets only web/dist/
    - job: test-api
      artifacts: false
  script: [./deploy-web.sh]
takeaways: needs: lets a job start as soon as its dependencies finish
needs: [] starts a job immediately
With needs, artifacts come only from the needed jobs
pitfalls: Needing a job that rules removed from this pipeline; mark it optional: true.

quiz.q: Job X has needs: [A]. A is in the build stage and finished; B in the build stage is still running. Does X start?
options: Yes, it only waits for A
No, it waits for the whole build stage
Only if X is in the build stage
quiz.explain: needs replaces stage ordering for that job; it waits only for the listed jobs.

concepts.name: Secrets: masked, protected and file variables
concepts.summary: Store credentials as CI/CD variables in GitLab's settings, mask them in logs, and give them only to protected branches.
concepts.why: Deploy passwords and keys must never live in the repository, and must not be readable from every branch.
concepts.body:
Passwords, keys and tokens (**credentials**) go in **Settings, CI/CD, Variables** of a project, a group or the whole GitLab server, never in `.gitlab-ci.yml`, which everyone with access to the repository can read. Each variable has options:

- **Masked**: the value is replaced with `[MASKED]` in job logs. To be maskable, a value must meet some length and character rules. **Masked and hidden** variables also can't be viewed again on GitLab's website after saving.
- **Protected**: only given to pipelines running on a **protected branch** or tag: one that only trusted people may push to (usually `main` and the branches used for releases). A developer pushing a feature branch can't read production credentials, because jobs on that branch simply don't receive them.
- **Environment scope**: only given to jobs that deploy to a matching environment, such as `production` (environments are covered at the Advanced level).
- **Type: File**: GitLab writes the value into a temporary file, and the variable holds that file's **path**. Ideal for tools that want a file, such as a login file for Kubernetes or a certificate.

The **job token**, `CI_JOB_TOKEN`, is a temporary password GitLab creates for each job. It lets the job use the project's package and container registries, and parts of GitLab's **API** (its interface for programs), for projects that allow it. It stops working when the job ends. An allowlist in the project settings controls which other projects accept it.

Masking is a safety net, not a guarantee: printing the secret base64-encoded, or only part of it, slips past the mask. And anyone who can push to a protected branch can make a job send protected variables anywhere, so choose carefully who may push there.
concepts.code:
deploy:
  image: $CI_REGISTRY/acme/tools/kubectl:1.33   # your own tools image
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH   # protected branch
  environment: production
  script:
    # KUBECONFIG is a protected, File-type variable: its value is a path
    - kubectl --kubeconfig "$KUBECONFIG" get nodes
    - ./notify.sh --token "$SLACK_TOKEN"   # masked: logs show [MASKED]

publish-package:
  script:
    - 'curl --header "JOB-TOKEN: $CI_JOB_TOKEN" --upload-file pkg.tgz
       "$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/packages/generic/pkg/1.0.0/pkg.tgz"'
takeaways: Secrets live in GitLab's CI/CD settings, not in the YAML file
Protected variables reach only protected branches and tags
File-type variables hold the path of a temporary file
pitfalls: Leaving a deploy secret unprotected, so any branch's pipeline can read it.

quiz.q: A protected variable is defined. A developer pushes to feature/x (unprotected). What does their job see?
quiz.explain: Protected variables are only passed to pipelines on protected branches or tags.

concepts.name: include, extends, !reference and components
concepts.summary: Split configuration into files, share templates across projects, inherit job settings with extends, and use CI/CD components.
concepts.why: Large projects and organisations need one maintained pipeline definition instead of copies pasted everywhere.
concepts.body:
**include** pulls other YAML files into your configuration:

- `include: local: ci/test.yml` from the same repository.
- `include: project: my-group/ci-templates`, `ref: v2`, `file: node.yml` from another project.
- `include: remote:` from a URL, and `include: template:` for templates that ship with GitLab.
- `include: component:` for CI/CD components.

**CI/CD components** are reusable, versioned pieces of pipeline configuration published in GitLab's **CI/CD Catalog**. A component declares its inputs (the values a user must or may give it, with their types) in a `spec:` header. You use it as `component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/my-group/components/python-test@1.2.0` with `inputs:`, where `$CI_SERVER_FQDN` is your GitLab server's address. Inputs are filled in with `$[[ inputs.name ]]` when the file is included, so mistakes are caught before the pipeline runs.

**Hidden jobs** have names starting with a dot (`.test-base`) and never run; they serve as templates. **extends** makes a job inherit from one or more of them, merging nested settings level by level. Lists such as `script` are **replaced**, not joined.

When you need just one piece of another job, **!reference** pulls in a specific value: `script: [!reference [.setup, script], make test]` combines lists that extends would overwrite.

Pin includes to a tag or a commit ID, like any dependency, and use the Pipeline editor's **Full configuration** view to see the final, merged result.
concepts.code:
include:
  - local: ci/lint.yml
  - project: acme/ci-templates
    ref: v2.3.0
    file: /templates/python.yml
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/acme/components/sast@1.4.0
    inputs:
      stage: test

.python-base:                     # hidden job: never runs on its own
  image: python:3.13
  before_script: [pip install -r requirements.txt]
  script: [echo base]

unit:
  extends: .python-base
  script: [pytest tests/unit]     # replaces the base script list

integration:
  extends: .python-base
  script:
    - !reference [.python-base, before_script]
    - pytest tests/integration
takeaways: include pulls in local, project, remote, template and component files
Hidden jobs plus extends give job templates; lists are replaced
Components are versioned, with typed inputs, and published in the CI/CD Catalog
pitfalls: Expecting extends to append to script; it overwrites the list. Use !reference to combine.

quiz.q: A job extends .base, which has script: [a]. The job defines script: [b]. What runs?
quiz.explain: extends merges nested settings, but lists such as script are replaced entirely.

concepts.name: Environments, manual deploys and review apps
concepts.summary: Track deployments with environment:, guard production with manual jobs and protected environments, and create review apps per merge request.
concepts.why: Knowing what is deployed where, and who may deploy to production, is central to shipping safely.
concepts.body:
An **environment** is a named place your app is deployed to, such as `staging` or `production`. Adding `environment:` to a job records a deployment each time the job runs. GitLab lists environments under **Operate, Environments**, with the commit currently deployed, the history, and a button to re-run an older successful deploy job. That re-run is your **rollback**: going back to the previous good version.

Key options:

- `name` and `url`: the URL appears as a link in merge requests.
- `deployment_tier`: production, staging, testing, development or other.
- `when: manual` in rules, so production deploys wait for a click.
- **Protected environments** (Settings, CI/CD) restrict who may run deploy jobs for them, and can require approval from chosen people.
- `resource_group: production` puts the job in a **resource group**: only one job of the group runs at a time, so two pipelines never deploy at once.

**Review apps** are temporary environments created per branch or merge request, so reviewers can try the change in a running copy. They're named with variables: `name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` (the branch name made safe for use in web addresses). A second job with `action: stop` removes the copy; link it with `on_stop`, and GitLab runs it when the branch is deleted or the merge request is merged. `auto_stop_in: 1 week` cleans up forgotten ones.

Environment-scoped variables let the same script deploy to staging or production with different credentials, chosen by the environment's name.
concepts.code:
deploy-review:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh "$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG"
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: https://$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.review.example.com
    on_stop: stop-review
    auto_stop_in: 1 week
  rules: [{if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"}]

stop-review:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./teardown.sh "$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG"
  environment: {name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG, action: stop}
  rules: [{if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event", when: manual}]

deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh production
  environment: {name: production, url: https://example.com}
  resource_group: production        # one deploy at a time
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual
takeaways: environment: records deployments and lets you roll back by re-running old jobs
Protected environments and manual rules guard production
resource_group allows one deploy at a time; on_stop cleans up review apps
pitfalls: Deploying production from two pipelines at once; add a resource_group.

options: Only maintainers can run the job
At most one job in that group runs at a time
The job runs on a production runner
quiz.explain: Jobs sharing a resource group are executed one at a time across pipelines.

concepts.name: Parent-child and multi-project pipelines
concepts.summary: Split big pipelines into child pipelines, generate configuration dynamically, and trigger pipelines in other projects.
concepts.why: Monorepos and systems of many services outgrow one flat pipeline; downstream pipelines keep them manageable.
concepts.body:
A **trigger job** starts another pipeline instead of running a script. The pipeline it starts is called a **downstream pipeline**.

- **Child pipelines** run in the same project: `trigger: include: path/to/child.yml`. Each child has its own stages and jobs, so a monorepo can have one child per service, each started only when its files change (`rules: changes`).
- **Multi-project pipelines** start a pipeline in another project: `trigger: project: acme/deployer`, with an optional `branch`. Useful when an app's pipeline must start a pipeline of an infrastructure project, or of end-to-end tests (tests of the whole system working together).

By default the trigger job succeeds as soon as the downstream pipeline is **created**. With `strategy: depend`, the trigger job waits and takes on the downstream pipeline's result, so a failing child fails the parent.

Dynamic child pipelines take this further: one job writes a YAML file (with a script or a template) and saves it as an artifact, and the trigger job includes it with `include: - artifact: generated.yml, job: generate`. This lets a pipeline create exactly the jobs needed, such as one per changed package.

Variables are passed downstream with `variables:` in the trigger job (`trigger:forward` controls what is forwarded). Child pipelines appear nested inside the parent's pipeline graph.
concepts.code:
generate:
  stage: build
  script:
    - ./ci/make-jobs.sh > child.yml    # writes one job per changed package
  artifacts: {paths: [child.yml]}
run-generated:
  stage: test
  trigger:
    include:
      - artifact: child.yml
        job: generate
    strategy: depend                   # parent fails if child fails
backend:
  trigger:
    include: services/backend/.gitlab-ci.yml
    strategy: depend
  rules:
    - changes: ["services/backend/**/*"]
e2e:
  stage: deploy
  variables: {APP_VERSION: $CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA}
  trigger:
    project: acme/e2e-tests
    branch: main
takeaways: trigger:include starts a child pipeline; trigger:project one in another project
strategy: depend makes the trigger job take on the downstream result
Dynamic child pipelines include YAML written by an earlier job
pitfalls: Forgetting strategy: depend and getting a green parent while the child fails.

quiz.q: Without strategy: depend, when does a trigger job succeed?
options: As soon as the downstream pipeline is created
When all its own scripts pass
quiz.explain: By default the trigger job only waits for the downstream pipeline to be created.

concepts.name: Runners and executors
concepts.summary: Install and register GitLab Runner, choose an executor, route jobs with tags, and tune how many jobs run at once.
concepts.why: Your own runners control cost, hardware, network access and security for every job you run.
concepts.body:
**GitLab Runner** is a single program (written in Go) that asks GitLab for jobs and runs them with an **executor**, the method it uses to run each job:

- `docker`: each job in a fresh container from the job's `image`. The usual choice.
- `kubernetes`: each job as a pod (Kubernetes' unit of running containers) in a Kubernetes cluster, so capacity grows with the cluster.
- `shell`: directly on the runner's machine. Simple, but jobs share the machine and anything earlier jobs left behind.
- `docker-autoscaler` and `instance`: create cloud virtual machines on demand through plugins; they replace the deprecated docker+machine autoscaling.

You create a runner on GitLab's website (for a project, a group or the whole server). That gives you a **token** starting with `glrt-`: a secret string proving the runner may connect. Then you run `gitlab-runner register` with it on the machine. The runner's settings live in `config.toml`, a settings file in the **TOML** format: `concurrent` caps how many jobs the whole runner process runs at once, and each `[[runners]]` section holds one executor's settings, such as the default image, `privileged` mode and mounted folders.

Jobs are routed with **runner tags**: a runner given the tags `gpu` and `linux` only takes jobs whose `tags:` are all among its own. A runner can also be allowed to take untagged jobs, or be limited to jobs from protected branches. Such a protected runner is the right place for deploy jobs with production access.

Security: `privileged = true` (needed for Docker-in-Docker) gives jobs the same power over the machine as its administrator. Keep such runners separate, and never share them with projects you don't trust.
concepts.code:
# Register a runner using the glrt- token from the UI
gitlab-runner register --non-interactive \
  --url https://gitlab.example.com \
  --token "$RUNNER_TOKEN" \
  --executor docker --docker-image alpine:3.22

# /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml (excerpt)
# concurrent = 8                 # max parallel jobs for this process
# [[runners]]
#   name = "docker-gpu"
#   executor = "docker"
#   [runners.docker]
#     image = "alpine:3.22"
#     privileged = false

# .gitlab-ci.yml side: route a job by tags
#   train:
#     tags: [gpu, linux]
gitlab-runner verify && gitlab-runner list
takeaways: The runner asks GitLab for jobs; the executor decides how each job is isolated
Runner tags route jobs; concurrent caps how many run at once
Privileged runners give jobs administrator power: keep them separate and protected
pitfalls: Using the shell executor for code you don't trust: jobs share the machine and whatever earlier jobs left on it.

quiz.q: A job has tags: [gpu]. Which runner can take it?
options: A runner whose tags include gpu
quiz.explain: All of a job's tags must be among the runner's tags.

concepts.name: ID tokens, OIDC and pipeline security
concepts.summary: Log in to clouds and Vault with id_tokens instead of stored keys, and close the common holes in pipeline security.
concepts.why: Whoever controls your pipeline controls your deploy credentials; logins without stored keys and strict protection rules limit the damage.
concepts.body:
A long-lived cloud password stored in CI/CD variables can be used for months by anyone who leaks it. `id_tokens:` avoids that. It makes GitLab give the job a signed **JWT** (JSON Web Token): a small piece of data, signed by GitLab, stating facts about the job. You choose its audience (`aud`: which service it is meant for).

The token's **claims**, the facts inside it, describe the job: `project_path`, `ref` (the branch or tag), `ref_protected`, `environment`, `pipeline_source`, and a `sub` (subject) such as `project_path:acme/shop:ref_type:branch:ref:main`.

A cloud provider (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) or HashiCorp Vault (a secrets manager) can be set up to trust your GitLab server as a token issuer, using **OpenID Connect** (OIDC), the standard for this kind of login. It then swaps the token for short-lived credentials. No long-lived keys are stored anywhere.

The **trust policy**, the cloud-side rule saying which tokens to accept, is where security lives. Require the exact `project_path`, and for production also `ref_protected: true` or a specific environment. Checking only the issuer would let every project on GitLab.com take on your cloud role.

Broader pipeline hardening:

- **Protect** the default branch, release branches and tags; protected variables, runners and environments all build on that.
- Merge requests from **forks** run their pipelines in the fork by default, without your secrets. Running them in your project is a deliberate, reviewed action.
- Keep the `CI_JOB_TOKEN` allowlist short.
- Pin included templates and components to versions: an attacker who can change a shared template changes every pipeline that includes it.
- Treat changes to `.gitlab-ci.yml` as security-sensitive, and require approval from code owners (named people who must review changes to certain files).
concepts.code:
deploy:
  image:
    name: amazon/aws-cli:2.27.0
    entrypoint: [""]           # the image would otherwise start the aws command
  id_tokens:
    AWS_TOKEN:
      aud: sts.amazonaws.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  environment: production
  script:
    - >
      export $(printf "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=%s AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=%s AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=%s"
      $(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity
      --role-arn "$ROLE_ARN" --role-session-name "gl-$CI_JOB_ID"
      --web-identity-token "$AWS_TOKEN" --duration-seconds 3600
      --query 'Credentials.[AccessKeyId,SecretAccessKey,SessionToken]' --output text))
    - aws sts get-caller-identity
# AWS trust policy condition (excerpt):
# "gitlab.example.com:sub": "project_path:acme/shop:ref_type:branch:ref:main"
takeaways: id_tokens give each job a signed JWT for logging in to clouds or Vault without stored keys
Restrict trust to project_path and protected refs
Protected branches underpin protected variables, runners and environments
pitfalls: A trust policy that only checks the issuer and audience, trusting every project on the GitLab server.

quiz.q: Which claim condition best ensures only main-branch jobs of acme/shop get production credentials?
quiz.explain: sub encodes both the project and the ref; aud and iss alone match every project.

concepts.name: Merge request pipelines and merge trains
concepts.summary: Understand branch, merge request and merged results pipelines, and how merge trains keep main passing when many merges happen.
concepts.why: In busy repositories, merge requests that pass on their own can still break main together; the right pipeline type prevents that.
concepts.body:
GitLab can create several kinds of pipeline for the same commit, and the difference matters:

- **Branch pipelines** run on the pushed commit, with `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == push`. They get protected variables only on protected branches.
- **Merge request pipelines** (`merge_request_event`) run on the merge request's source branch when it is opened or updated. Jobs need rules that match this source. They get `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_*` variables, such as the merge request's number (`CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID`) and its target branch.
- **Merged results pipelines** run on a temporary commit that merges the source branch into the **current** target branch, so the tests see the code as it will be after merging.
- **Merge trains** queue merge requests. Each one's pipeline runs on the target branch plus every merge request ahead of it in the train. If one fails, it's removed and the ones behind it restart. As each pipeline passes, its merge request merges in order, so main keeps passing even with many merges at once.

Without `workflow:rules`, a push to a branch with an open merge request can create both a branch pipeline and a merge request pipeline, doubling the cost. The `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS` never-rule prevents that.

Merged results pipelines and merge trains need GitLab's paid Premium tier and a project setting. `interruptible: true` lets GitLab cancel a running pipeline automatically once a newer push has made it pointless, saving runner time.
concepts.code:
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

default:
  interruptible: true            # cancel pipelines a newer push made pointless

test:
  script:
    - echo "MR !$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID into $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME"
    - make test
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

deploy:
  interruptible: false           # never cancel a deploy midway
  script: [./deploy.sh]
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
takeaways: Branch, merge request, merged results and merge train pipelines test different commits
Merge trains test each merge request on top of the ones queued ahead of it
workflow:rules prevents duplicate branch and merge request pipelines
pitfalls: Writing rules only for branch pipelines, so jobs silently vanish from merge request pipelines.

quiz.q: Two merge requests each pass their own pipeline but break main when both merge. What prevents this?
options: Merge trains, which test each merge request on top of the ones ahead of it
quiz.explain: Merge trains validate the combination of queued changes before they merge.
